title: We built an RTS with AI assistance. The supply trucks taught us what our tests were missing.
author: Key_Art_9961
selftext:
We’re Knowhubs, the developers of Battlegroup Sea Lines. We used AI to help write the Godot code and ChatGPT Images for the menu illustration and button surfaces. One of the most revealing tests was simply starting a skirmish with a mouse. A supply truck could complete its route once it had an order, but a starting truck could sit there waiting for the player to give it one. That felt wrong the moment we played.



We changed the opening so that, once you deploy the mobile HQ, the trucks collect from supplies you’ve actually discovered and can reach. You can still give a truck a manual order. In our release playtest they delivered 520 supplies while we placed a barracks, changed its rally point and trained two squads.



For anyone building games with AI-assisted code, what do you put in the very first minute of a human playtest? Ours is now “deploy the HQ and give the trucks no orders.” It catches a different problem from asking whether a truck can follow a route.



The Windows Early Access build is free, with optional tips. Start with Coastal Skirmish if you want to try the opening. [https://knowhubs.itch.io/battlegroup-sea-lines](https://knowhubs.itch.io/battlegroup-sea-lines)

comments.author: Almaravarion
comments.body:
And apparently You never learned a single thing with trucks, as even simple check for naval variant of the same problem is still manual only.

The dreadful part is it's 'early access' rather than 'tech demo'.

replies.author: Key_Art_9961
replies.body: I'm only learning my friend,  that the kind of feedback I was looking for sorry the terminology I didn't know there was a difference we all have to start somewhere

replies.author: Almaravarion
replies.body:
"I am only learning my friend" - that is the part I am doubting here.

While yes, we are all learning in the process of making new things, and no one is not making mistakes, the reason why I doubt is the following:  
\- You encountered a problem - manual movement of cargo with trucks  
\- You fixed it - automated them  
\- You FAILED to learn from this problem, and failed to check if the problem is present elsewhere - in near 1:1 reimplementation for example - in case of naval cargo units.

Frankly to me it sounds like treating not only - cargo units for navy and land as separate entities with separate codebase, but also - considering them both as separate conceptually, to the point where You failed to connect that problem in one is the same the other has with different pathing. Not only You, but also all other 'developers' IF they exist. 

This is why I made a claim that You found a problem, fixed it, but FAILED to learn from it a single thing.

replies.author: Key_Art_9961
replies.body: Overthinking it my friend,  there are levels we are starting out and we will continue to work on it thank you for your feedback

replies.author: Almaravarion
replies.body:
Here's your second problem - You are unable or unwilling to take accountability for that failure. Sit down and acknowledge 'well, shit, I fucked up, I failed to learn from that mistake, maybe there are other places where I did the same thing, and I should review the data we already have".

Good luck. You'll need it, but it will not save your project alone.
